theory.overview: Symmetric encryption powers the secure communication we rely on every day—from messaging apps to banking transactions. Unlike classical ciphers that operate letter by letter, modern symmetric ciphers process data in blocks using complex substitution-permutation networks. At their heart lies the fundamental principle: the same secret key both locks (encrypts) and unlocks (decrypts) the message. This creates a challenge—how do you securely share the key?—which we'll solve later with asymmetric cryptography. For now, understand that symmetric encryption provides speed and strength: AES-256, the current standard, withstands all known attacks even from nation-state adversaries with supercomputers.

sections.title: From Classical to Modern
sections.content: Classical ciphers failed because they preserved statistical patterns—letter frequencies in ciphertext mirrored plaintext. Modern symmetric ciphers solve this through confusion (obscuring the relationship between key and ciphertext) and diffusion (spreading plaintext influence across entire ciphertext). Claude Shannon established these principles in 1949. Confusion means changing one key bit should change about half the ciphertext bits. Diffusion means changing one plaintext bit should affect many ciphertext bits. Together they create avalanche effect: tiny input changes cause completely different outputs, defeating frequency analysis completely.
keyPoints: Confusion: Complex relationship between key and ciphertext
Diffusion: Each plaintext bit affects many ciphertext bits
Avalanche effect: Small input change → completely different output
Statistical patterns in plaintext are hidden in ciphertext

sections.title: Block Ciphers
sections.content: Modern encryption operates on fixed-size blocks—typically 128 bits (16 bytes)—rather than individual characters. If plaintext is longer than one block, we use modes of operation to chain blocks together securely. The core block cipher transforms an n-bit plaintext block into an n-bit ciphertext block using a secret key. This transformation must be reversible (for decryption) but computationally indistinguishable from random without the key. Block ciphers iterate multiple rounds of substitution and permutation, with each round using a subkey derived from the main key through a key schedule algorithm.
keyPoints: Fixed block size: AES uses 128 bits, DES used 64 bits
Multiple rounds (10-14) of substitution and permutation
Subkeys generated from master key via key schedule

sections.title: AES: The Modern Standard
sections.content: The Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) replaced DES in 2001 after a global competition. AES operates on 128-bit blocks with keys of 128, 192, or 256 bits. It uses a substitution-permutation network with 10-14 rounds depending on key size. Each round consists of four operations: SubBytes (byte substitution using lookup table), ShiftRows (transposition), MixColumns (diffusion through matrix multiplication), and AddRoundKey (XOR with round key). No practical attack exists against full AES—brute forcing a 256-bit key would require more energy than exists in the observable universe. AES powers TLS/SSL (HTTPS), VPNs, disk encryption, and virtually all secure digital communication.
keyPoints: AES-128: 10 rounds, AES-192: 12 rounds, AES-256: 14 rounds
Each round: SubBytes → ShiftRows → MixColumns → AddRoundKey
Final round omits MixColumns for reversibility

sections.title: Modes of Operation
sections.content: Raw block ciphers only encrypt single blocks. To encrypt longer messages, we use modes of operation. ECB (Electronic Codebook) encrypts each block independently—identical plaintext blocks produce identical ciphertext, revealing patterns. Never use ECB. CBC (Cipher Block Chaining) XORs each plaintext block with the previous ciphertext block before encrypting, propagating changes through the chain. CTR (Counter) mode turns a block cipher into a stream cipher by encrypting incrementing counters and XORing with plaintext. CTR allows parallel encryption/decryption and is widely used today. GCM (Galois/Counter Mode) adds authentication, providing both confidentiality and integrity verification.
keyPoints: ECB: Never use—identical blocks → identical ciphertext
CBC: Chaining with IV, sequential processing required
CTR: Parallelizable, treats block cipher as stream cipher

keyConcepts.name: Confusion and Diffusion
keyConcepts.latex: Confusion: complex key-ciphertext relationship, Diffusion: spread plaintext influence

complexity.encryption: O(n) for n-bit message, constant per block

steps.title: Prepare Data and Key
steps.description: Convert plaintext to 128-bit blocks. Pad if necessary. Generate or load encryption key.

steps.title: Initial Round - AddRoundKey
steps.description: XOR the plaintext block with the first round key (derived from master key).

steps.title: SubBytes Transformation
steps.description: Substitute each byte using the AES S-box lookup table. Provides non-linearity.
steps.latex: For each byte b: b' = S-Box[b]

steps.title: ShiftRows
steps.description: Shift each row of the state matrix cyclically. Row 0: no shift, Row 1: 1 byte left, Row 2: 2 bytes, Row 3: 3 bytes.

steps.title: MixColumns
steps.description: Mix each column using matrix multiplication in GF(2^8). Spreads influence across columns.
steps.latex: Each column multiplied by fixed matrix in Galois Field

steps.title: Repeat Rounds
steps.description: Perform SubBytes → ShiftRows → MixColumns → AddRoundKey for rounds 2 through 13.
steps.latex: Repeat for rounds 2 to N-1 (round 2-13 for AES-256)

steps.title: Final Round
steps.description: Final round omits MixColumns. Perform SubBytes → ShiftRows → AddRoundKey.

practiceProblems.title: Block Size Calculation
practiceProblems.description: How many 128-bit AES blocks are needed to encrypt a 1000-byte message?
hints: AES block size is 128 bits = 16 bytes
Divide message size by block size
Round up to nearest whole block

solution.explanation: 1000 bytes / 16 bytes per block = 62.5 → rounded up to 63 blocks. Last block needs padding.

practiceProblems.title: ECB vs CBC Pattern
practiceProblems.description: You encrypt an image using ECB mode. What pattern will be visible in the ciphertext?
practiceProblems.latex: ECB(plaintext) = identical blocks produce identical ciphertext
hints: Large uniform areas in image remain recognizable

solution.answer: The original image structure remains visible because identical pixel blocks produce identical ciphertext blocks
solution.explanation: ECB does not hide patterns. This is why ECB is insecure and should never be used for anything important.

practiceProblems.title: Brute Force Time
practiceProblems.description: A supercomputer can try 10^15 keys per second. How long would it take to brute force AES-128?

solution.explanation: 3.4 × 10^38 keys ÷ 10^15 keys/sec = 3.4 × 10^23 seconds ≈ 10^13 years. For comparison, the universe is 1.4 × 10^10 years old.

practiceProblems.title: Avalanche Effect
practiceProblems.description: If you flip one bit in the plaintext, approximately what percentage of ciphertext bits should change in a good cipher?
hints: 50% is the ideal for random-like behavior

solution.explanation: In a well-designed cipher like AES, changing one input bit should change about half the output bits on average. This creates the avalanche effect.

practiceProblems.title: Key Schedule
practiceProblems.description: Why does AES use a key schedule to generate round keys instead of using the master key directly?
hints: Each round needs its own 128-bit key

solution.answer: The key schedule provides different subkeys for each round, preventing attacks that exploit round similarities and ensuring proper mixing of key material throughout the cipher
solution.explanation: Using the same key for all rounds would make the cipher vulnerable to slide attacks and other cryptanalytic techniques. The key schedule ensures each round has unique, related-but-different key material.

practiceProblems.title: Mode Selection
practiceProblems.description: Which mode should you use for: (a) Random access to encrypted database records, (b) Streaming video encryption, (c) Secure messaging with integrity?
hints: CTR is also good for streaming (parallelizable)

solution.explanation: CTR mode allows decrypting any block independently. GCM combines CTR encryption with authentication for integrity verification—essential for secure messaging.

snippets.title: AES Encryption with PyCryptodome
snippets.code:
from Crypto.Cipher import AES
from Crypto.Util.Padding import pad
import os

# Generate a random 256-bit key
key = os.urandom(32)  # 32 bytes = 256 bits

# Generate random IV for CBC mode
iv = os.urandom(16)   # 16 bytes = 128 bits

# Create cipher and encrypt
cipher = AES.new(key, AES.MODE_CBC, iv=iv)
plaintext = b"Secret message here!"
padded = pad(plaintext, AES.block_size)
ciphertext = cipher.encrypt(padded)

print(f"Ciphertext: {ciphertext.hex()}")

# Decrypt
decipher = AES.new(key, AES.MODE_CBC, iv=iv)
decrypted = decipher.decrypt(ciphertext)
print(f"Decrypted: {decrypted}")

snippets.title: AES-GCM (Authenticated Encryption)
snippets.code:
from Crypto.Cipher import AES
import os

key = os.urandom(32)
nonce = os.urandom(12)  # GCM uses nonce instead of IV

# GCM provides encryption AND authentication
cipher = AES.new(key, AES.MODE_GCM, nonce=nonce)

# Associated data (authenticated but not encrypted)
cipher.update(b"header data")

plaintext = b"Secret message"
ciphertext, tag = cipher.encrypt_and_digest(plaintext)

print(f"Ciphertext: {ciphertext.hex()}")
print(f"Auth tag: {tag.hex()}")  # 16 bytes authentication tag

# Decryption verifies the tag automatically
decipher = AES.new(key, AES.MODE_GCM, nonce=nonce)
decipher.update(b"header data")
decrypted = decipher.decrypt_and_verify(ciphertext, tag)
print(f"Verified: {decrypted}")
